Hosting an Iskra server

Last updated 17 October 2026

On this page
  • 1. From the desktop app
  • 2. The standalone server
  • Reaching your server from the internet
  • Backups, moving and importing
  • server.json reference
  • What's in the folder

Your server, your choice. Iskra charges nothing; this is just a guide. The one exception: the app's DigitalOcean sign-up link is Iskra's referral link (Iskra gets a little DigitalOcean credit, you pay nothing extra), and the app says so.

An Iskra server is a folder. Everything lives in it: settings, members, messages, files and keys. Back it up from the app with one click and restore it on any machine (see Backups, moving and importing).

There are three ways to run one:

Best for Friends can join from
The desktop app (Windows, macOS and Linux) Trying it out, LAN parties, friends at home or anywhere Desktop app; any browser and phone once it's open to the internet
The standalone server on your PC Always-on server at home Desktop app; any browser and phone once it's open to the internet
The standalone server on a VPS (Linux) Friends all over the place, 24/7, or when your home connection can't host (rent one from the app, or from the DigitalOcean Marketplace) Desktop app and any browser (with HTTPS)

Want a small always-on box at home (an old PC, a mini PC or a Raspberry Pi)? See An Iskra box at home.

1. From the desktop app#

Install Iskra, click Create a server, pick a name and a starting point (a starter template: Gaming group, Friends hangout, Board games and tabletop or Empty). Done: the server runs on your PC (voice included) while the app is open, and you're its owner. Click Invite friends to get a link.

  • Its folder is Documents\Iskra\Servers\<name> (on macOS: ~/Library/Application Support/Iskra/Servers/<name>).
  • Friends on the same network can join right away. For friends elsewhere, turn on Let friends anywhere join in Server settings → Internet access (see Reaching your server from the internet).
  • The server stops when you quit the app. Tick Keep my server running (when it's created, or in Server settings → Internet access): Iskra then starts with your computer, hidden in the tray, and starts that server; closing the window keeps it running. Untick it on the last such server and Iskra stops starting with the computer too.

2. The standalone server#

Download iskra-server for Windows, Linux or macOS and unpack it: win-x64, linux-x64, linux-arm64 (Raspberry Pi 4 and 5 with a 64-bit system, and other 64-bit ARM boards), osx-arm64 or osx-x64. Voice (LiveKit) is included. For a box that runs it all the time, see An Iskra box at home.

shell
iskra-server my-server        # Windows: iskra-server.exe my-server
  • The folder my-server is created on first run.
  • The server prints a one-time owner link (also saved as my-server/owner-invite.txt). Open it in the Iskra app or at app.iskra.foo to become the owner. The file disappears once used.
  • Stop the server with Ctrl+C. Start it again with the same command; everything is kept.
  • Start from a template: iskra-server my-server --template gaming (see Starter templates).

Keep it running (start with the computer)#

shell
iskra-server install-autostart my-server     # and to undo it: iskra-server remove-autostart my-server

Nothing starts right away (stop the copy in your terminal first, then use the "start it now" command it prints). What it sets up:

System What When it starts
Windows A scheduled task, Iskra server <folder>-<hash>, running without a window (conhost --headless), its log in logs/ (errors also in server.log), restarted if it crashes, no time limit When you log in. Run from an administrator terminal and it starts with the computer instead, before anyone logs in (as you, without storing your password: "S4U"; never with administrator rights)
Linux A systemd user service, ~/.config/systemd/user/iskra-<folder>-<hash>.service, enabled When you log in. loginctl enable-linger $USER makes it start at boot. As root it refuses: use the system unit below
macOS A launchd agent, ~/Library/LaunchAgents/foo.iskra.server.<folder>-<hash>.plist, its log in logs/ (errors also in server.log), restarted if it crashes When you log in

Installing and removing are written to the server's security log.

Starter templates#

A new server can start with channels of every kind, who can see and use them, roles, rules and settings from a template. It's applied once, on the first start of a new server. Built in: gaming, friends, tabletop, empty; list them with iskra-server templates.

  • In the desktop app: the second step of Create a server (or From a template file…), with a preview.
  • Standalone: iskra-server my-server --template gaming, or "Template": "gaming" (or a .json path) in server.json before the first start.
  • Your own: Server settings → Overview → Save as template, or write one (templates don't carry the server's icon and banner). Check a file with iskra-server templates ./book-club.json.
  • Add a template to a server already in use (additive only, stop the server first): iskra-server templates apply my-server ./more-channels.json, then again with --apply.

The format, with an example, is in Server templates.

Rent a small server#

When your home connection can't host (carrier-grade NAT, or a router you can't change), a small virtual server at a hosting company runs Iskra for your group all the time. The app walks you through it: Server settings → Internet access → Rent a small server (it's the first option when Iskra finds a shared connection). No terminal needed; about 15 minutes. Your group picks the provider, pays it and owns the server; nothing goes to Iskra. The desktop app can also do all of it on DigitalOcean for you: see Rent a server on DigitalOcean.

  1. Make an account at a VPS provider, for example Hetzner or DigitalOcean.
  2. Create a server: Ubuntu 24.04 LTS (or Debian 12), x86-64, the cheapest plan (about €4–6 a month).
  3. Paste the app's setup text into the User data box (Hetzner: "Cloud config"; DigitalOcean: "Advanced options → Add initialization scripts") and create the server.
  4. Paste the server's IPv4 address into the app and press Connect. The app waits while the server installs (usually 3–10 minutes, at most 20), checks that it really is the server you set up, and makes you its owner.

What the setup text does (a bash script that cloud-init runs once, as root, on first boot; its log is /var/log/iskra-setup.log):

  • downloads iskra-server-<version>-linux-x64.tar.gz (the version of your app) and SHA256SUMS.txt from the release on GitHub over HTTPS, and stops unless the package matches its checksum;
  • unpacks it into /opt/iskra, owned by a new system user iskra, and installs the systemd service shown below (restarts on failure, automatic updates on);
  • opens only 22/tcp (SSH, so your provider's tools keep working), 80/tcp, 443/tcp, 7881/tcp and 7882/udp with ufw;
  • writes server.json with HTTPS on for <your-ip-with-dashes>.sslip.io (a free certificate from Let's Encrypt), your server's name and starting point, and a one-time owner key.

The owner key. The app makes 32 random bytes, OwnerClaim in server.json. On its first start the server moves it out of server.json into owner-claim (readable by the server only) and makes the owner invite from it; the key and that invite are never written to a log. The app checks a proof made with the key before it trusts the server (so a different server at that address can't pretend), then joins as owner, and the key is deleted. Until then the app keeps the key in its encrypted store (like your account keys; protected by the system keychain in the desktop app), so closing the dialog doesn't lose it; Start over with a new owner key deletes it. Keep the setup text to yourself until then; afterwards it's useless. Your provider can see the setup text (like everything on a server you rent from them).

Rather use a terminal? The same dialog has Copy a prompt for an AI assistant with these steps, and no keys in it. Without the app's key you become the owner the usual way: journalctl -u iskra shows the link (also in /opt/iskra/world/owner-invite.txt).

Moving an existing server there takes a terminal for now: make a backup, copy it to the server, stop the service, restore it into /opt/iskra/world (empty the new folder first), chown -R iskra:iskra /opt/iskra, start it again, then use Move this server so everyone follows.

Rent a server on DigitalOcean (one click)#

The desktop app can rent and set up the server in your own DigitalOcean account: Create a server → Rent one on DigitalOcean (also offered in Rent a small server). You pay DigitalOcean directly, about $6 a month for their smallest server that fits Iskra (1 GB memory; the app shows the exact price from DigitalOcean's size list before anything is created). Iskra charges nothing, runs nothing for your server and never sees it, your token or your card. The account link is Iskra's DigitalOcean referral link, and the app says so: Iskra gets some DigitalOcean credit, which helps pay for its own server, and new DigitalOcean accounts get signup credit.

  1. Account. Make a DigitalOcean account, or use the one you have.

  2. Access. Connect to DigitalOcean opens your browser: sign in and allow Iskra. The app uses OAuth for a desktop app (authorization code with PKCE, no client secret): your browser comes back to a one-time listener on 127.0.0.1 (this computer only, a random port, closed right after), and the app swaps the code for a key that works for one hour. It asks only for droplet:create droplet:read droplet:delete firewall:create firewall:read firewall:delete regions:read sizes:read tag:create. Or use an API token: in DigitalOcean, API → Tokens → Generate New Token, the shortest expiration (30 days, or Custom), Custom Scopes with only droplet (create, read, delete), firewall (create, read, delete), regions (read), sizes (read) and tag (create), and paste it into the app.

  3. Server. Pick a location (the app guesses the nearest from your time zone), a name and a starting point. SSH stays closed unless you tick Also allow SSH.

  4. Create. The app creates, through DigitalOcean's API (api.digitalocean.com, HTTPS):

    • a droplet iskra-<name>: Ubuntu 24.04, the cheapest basic size with at least 1 GB, tag iskra, monitoring and DigitalOcean's paid backups off, with the same setup text as user data (it carries the one-time owner key, turns on automatic updates and daily backups);
    • a cloud firewall iskra-<name>-firewall for that droplet only: in 80/tcp, 443/tcp, 7881/tcp, 7882/udp (plus 22/tcp only if you asked), out everything.

    Then it waits for the droplet's IPv4 address (up to 5 minutes) and for https://<ip-with-dashes>.sslip.io/health to answer with a valid Let's Encrypt certificate (up to 25 minutes), checks the owner proof and joins you as owner.

  5. Your server document. Save your server document saves a Markdown file (in your language) with the address, how friends join, where your keys and recovery live, the monthly cost and how to cancel, how updates, backups and moving work, what Iskra can and can't see, and a ready-to-copy prompt for an AI assistant that describes the setup exactly (Ubuntu version, the iskra service, /opt/iskra, ports, logs). It holds no token, keys or passwords.

The key stays on your computer. The OAuth key or pasted token lives only in the desktop app's main process memory: it's sent only to api.digitalocean.com, never shown back to the page, logged or written to disk, and forgotten when setup finishes, the dialog closes, the page reloads, or after two hours at most. You can also delete a pasted token in DigitalOcean afterwards.

If something fails the app says what went wrong (in DigitalOcean's own words too) and, if a droplet was already created, offers Delete it at DigitalOcean (the firewall, then the droplet). Closing the dialog during setup asks whether to delete or keep what was made; nothing paid is left behind without asking. If the server is slow to answer, Keep waiting tries for another 20 minutes.

SSH. Closed by default: nobody needs to log in to run Iskra. To use SSH or DigitalOcean's Droplet Console, add an inbound rule for TCP 22 to the droplet's firewall (Networking → Firewalls); ufw on the droplet already allows it.

Cancelling. Destroy the droplet in DigitalOcean (Droplets → the droplet → Destroy); a switched-off droplet still costs money. Then delete its firewall. Make a backup first if you want to keep the history.

DigitalOcean Marketplace#

Started on DigitalOcean's website rather than in the app? The Iskra 1-Click image makes the same kind of server without a terminal. You pay DigitalOcean directly (about $6 a month for the 1 GB droplet); Iskra charges nothing and never sees the server. DigitalOcean doesn't build or support Iskra.

Iskra isn't in the DigitalOcean Marketplace yet. Until it is, Rent a server on DigitalOcean in the desktop app does the same in one go.

  1. Open Iskra in the DigitalOcean Marketplace and press Create Iskra Droplet.

  2. Pick a region near your group and the $6 size (1 GB). DigitalOcean asks for a password or an SSH key: pick either, you won't need it for Iskra. Create the droplet; it's ready in about a minute.

  3. Open the droplet's Console in DigitalOcean. It shows the server's address and a claim code:

    Address:     https://203-0-113-7.sslip.io
Claim code:  7KQ2-ZM8P-X4TD-9HRA   (works once, until 2026-10-15 12:00 UTC)

    The same text is in /root/iskra-claim.txt and in the message you see when you log in.

  4. In the Iskra app (desktop, phone or app.iskra.foo): Join a server → Claim it, enter the address and the code, and press Check. The app shows the server's name and key; Join as owner makes you its owner.

What the droplet runs. Ubuntu 24.04 LTS with the Iskra server in /opt/iskra as the iskra user and the systemd service shown below (sandboxed by systemd: it can write only under /opt/iskra and a private /tmp), HTTPS for <ip-with-dashes>.sslip.io, automatic updates and daily backups on, security updates for Ubuntu (unattended-upgrades) on, and ufw letting in only 22/tcp, 80/tcp, 443/tcp, 7881/tcp and 7882/udp. The image holds no keys: on first boot each droplet writes its own server.json (/var/lib/cloud/scripts/per-instance/10-iskra-world, log in /var/log/iskra-setup.log), and the server makes its keys and certificate itself.

The claim code. The server makes it on its first start ("OwnerClaim": "generate" in server.json): 16 letters and digits (80 random bits), shown only on the console and kept in owner-claim-code.txt (owner-only). It works once, for 24 hours. The app never sends the code anywhere: it derives a key from it and checks the server's proof, exactly like Rent a small server does with its owner key. Once you've joined, the code and the setting are gone and the console goes back to normal. If the code expired first, restart the server (DigitalOcean: Power → Power cycle, or systemctl restart iskra on the console) and a fresh one appears. Making a code is written to the security log; the code itself never is.

Changing things later. Your own domain: point it at the droplet and set Https.Domain (and PublicUrl) in /opt/iskra/world/server.json, then systemctl restart iskra. Cancelling works as above: destroy the droplet.

On a Linux VPS with systemd#

shell
sudo useradd --system --create-home --home-dir /opt/iskra iskra
sudo tar -xzf iskra-server-*-linux-x64.tar.gz -C /opt/iskra --strip-components=1
sudo chown -R iskra:iskra /opt/iskra

/etc/systemd/system/iskra.service:

ini
[Unit]
Description=Iskra server
After=network-online.target

[Service]
User=iskra
WorkingDirectory=/opt/iskra
# Undoes an automatic update that doesn't start (see Updating). Optional, but needed for automatic updates.
ExecStartPre=-/opt/iskra/iskra-update-guard
ExecStart=/opt/iskra/iskra-server /opt/iskra/world
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5
# Lets the server use ports 80 and 443 without running as root.
AmbientCapabilities=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
shell
sudo systemctl enable --now iskra
sudo journalctl -u iskra -f        # shows the owner link on first start

Restarting without friends seeing "went offline". systemd stops the server the same way for a restart as for a stop, so by default members see "<server> went offline". Say it's a restart first, and they see "restarting, hold on" and are back within seconds:

shell
sudo -u iskra /opt/iskra/iskra-server expect-restart /opt/iskra/world --reason update --eta 30
sudo systemctl restart iskra

expect-restart leaves a small marker (restart-expected) in the server folder holding only the reason (update or restart, the default) and the expected downtime in seconds (--eta, 0–600, optional). The server reads it as it stops and deletes it; a marker older than 2 minutes is ignored, so a restart that didn't happen doesn't turn a later stop into "restarting". Put it in your own update scripts just before the restart. Or make systemctl reload iskra the friendly restart by adding this to the unit:

ini
ExecReload=/opt/iskra/iskra-server expect-restart /opt/iskra/world
ExecReload=+/bin/systemctl --no-block restart %n

Updating#

As the owner, open Server settings → Server updates. It shows the version the server runs and whether a newer one is out (the owner also gets a short notice above the chat). Choose what happens when one is:

What it does Where
Off Never looks for new versions Everywhere
Tell me (default) Looks at GitHub releases every 6 hours and tells you Everywhere
Install automatically Also installs it, in the hour after a time you pick (04:00 by default, server time), once nobody is in a voice channel. Update now installs it right away Linux, run by systemd as above

Installing by hand (Windows, macOS, or "Tell me"): stop the server, unpack the new iskra-server package over the old files (the server folder, e.g. my-server, isn't in the package and stays as it is), start it again. A server started by the desktop app updates together with the app and never checks by itself.

How an automatic update works:

  1. The server downloads the package for its system (iskra-server-<version>-linux-x64.tar.gz) and the release's SHA256SUMS.txt, from github.com/quikmn/iskra-voice over HTTPS only.
  2. It checks the package's SHA-256 against SHA256SUMS.txt and against the checksum GitHub lists for the file, verifies its signed build attestation (see the trust model below), and that the archive holds nothing but plain files at its top level. It runs the new iskra-server version to make sure it starts on this machine. Anything that doesn't match stops the update; nothing has been replaced yet.
  3. It swaps the new files in (the old ones go to .update/previous/ next to iskra-server), tells everyone "restarting for an update", and exits; systemd starts the new version a few seconds later. Members' apps reconnect by themselves.
  4. The new version confirms itself after running for a minute. If it fails to start three times before that, iskra-update-guard puts the previous version back and the owner sees "the update didn't start"; that version isn't tried again automatically.

Every check you start, change of setting, install, failure, finished update and rollback is written to the security log (Server settings → Sign-ins & security).

Automatic updates need: the systemd unit above with the ExecStartPre line (Server settings → Server updates says so if it's missing; iskra-update-guard comes in the Linux package), and the server's user owning the folder iskra-server is in (chown -R iskra:iskra /opt/iskra). Updates never touch the world folder. Database changes in new versions are forward-only, so a rolled-back version runs on a database the new one may already have migrated; that's why a version only confirms after it has started cleanly, and why daily backups exist.

What the checks prove (trust model). The download comes over TLS from GitHub, and the checksums come from the same GitHub release. That catches corrupted or truncated downloads and anyone tampering between GitHub and you. It does not protect against someone who can publish releases on the Iskra repository, since they could replace the package and SHA256SUMS.txt together. For that, releases carry build-provenance attestations, and the server verifies them itself before installing (on by default: Check the signed build attestation). It gets the Sigstore bundles for the exact file from GitHub and checks them on the server, with Sigstore's root built into Iskra: the signature must come from Iskra's release workflow running on GitHub's own runners for this version (not from a person's account), be in Sigstore's public transparency log, and name this file with its SHA-256. Someone who only gets into the GitHub account can still publish a release, but can't make a matching attestation for a changed file without also changing the release workflow, which shows in the public log. A release without an attestation (or one that doesn't verify) is never installed automatically; Server settings → Server updates says why, and you can install it by hand. Turning the check off (in Server settings → Server updates, or "VerifyAttestation": false in server.json) is logged and shows a warning. Sigstore adds new signing keys now and then; a server too old to know a new one refuses that update with "doesn't verify" until you update it by hand once. To check a file yourself: gh attestation verify <file> -R quikmn/iskra-voice. If you'd rather review every release first, use Tell me.

The server only asks GitHub's public API (no account; 60 requests an hour per IP, and an unchanged list doesn't count), and tells GitHub nothing beyond what any request does (its IP address) and its version in the User-Agent.

Health check#

GET /health answers {"iskra":1,"status":"ok","version":"…","uptimeSeconds":…,"voice":"up"} (voice is up, down or off): nothing private, for an uptime monitor. GET / answers {"iskra":1,"name":…} as before.

Reaching your server from the internet#

One switch: Let friends anywhere join#

As the owner, open Server settings → Internet access in the app and turn on Let friends anywhere join. This works the same for a server in the desktop app and for the standalone server at home. Iskra then:

  1. Asks your router to open the ports (UPnP or NAT-PMP): outside 80/tcp and 443/tcp to the server's port, and voice 7881/tcp and 7882/udp (your Voice ports). It keeps them open while the server runs and closes them when it stops.
  2. Gives your server a free address that points at your public IP, like 203-0-113-7.sslip.io.
  3. Gets a real HTTPS certificate for it from Let's Encrypt, so friends can join from any browser, phone included.
  4. Tells voice your public address.

A checklist shows how each step went, in plain words. New invite links use the public address. Iskra re-checks every few minutes, so a router restart or a new IP from your provider is picked up by itself.

Below it, What Iskra found out: whether your router has its own public address, a shared one (carrier-grade NAT, 100.64.0.0/10) or another private one (a second router or your provider's NAT in front: double NAT), whether it refused some ports, its make and model when UPnP says, and the exact voice ports. All of this comes from your router's own answers and your computer; no outside service is asked.

Forward the ports yourself lists, step by step, your router's settings page (its address on your network), this computer's address, and every port with its protocol. Copy a prompt for an AI assistant fills in a question for ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude or any other assistant with your system, router model, those two local addresses and the ports, and shows it in a box you can edit before copying. It never includes your public address, keys or invite links.

When it can't work, it says why:

  • Your router doesn't answer (UPnP is off): turn on UPnP in the router's settings, or forward the ports it lists by hand, then press Check again.
  • The router won't open port 80 (many only allow ports above 1024): forward port 80 by hand. Until then friends with the desktop app can join over plain HTTP; browsers need HTTPS.
  • Carrier-grade NAT: some providers share one public address between customers (your router's "public" address is then in 100.64.0.0/10 or another private range). Port forwarding on your own router can't help: the provider's NAT sits in front of it. Friends behind such a connection can always join a reachable server; only the person hosting needs an open connection. The app lists the options, quickest first:
    1. Let friends connect without port forwarding (experimental, the desktop app or a standalone server), nothing to open and nothing to install.
    2. Rent a small server, ready in about 15 minutes, paid and owned by your group.
    3. Check whether you already have a public IPv4 address (many fiber connections do): the check shows what your router says.
    4. Ask your provider for a public IPv4 address. Often free and done once; mobile broadband (4G/5G) almost never gets one.
    5. Use Tailscale (free): a free app that links your group's devices as if they were on one network. Everyone installs it once; no ports to open.
    6. Let someone in your group with an open connection host: the server is one folder, so move it.

What "reachable" means. Iskra doesn't use outside services to test your server, so it only reports what it can actually prove: verified once Let's Encrypt has connected to your server from the internet, or checked through your router when the server can reach itself via your public address. Otherwise it says it hasn't been confirmed from outside; send a friend an invite to try.

Why sslip.io. sslip.io (and its twin nip.io) is a long-running free wildcard DNS service: 1-2-3-4.sslip.io resolves to 1.2.3.4, with nothing to sign up for. Let's Encrypt issues certificates for its names and has granted it a very large rate limit (sslip.io isn't on the Public Suffix List, so all its users share the per-domain limit; the operators have had it raised to 250,000 certificates a week). The address follows your IP, so if your provider changes it, the address and certificate change too and older invite links stop working. For stable links, use your own domain (a free dynamic-DNS name works) and set it as Internet.Domain.

Prefer to forward ports yourself? Set "PortMapping": false and your Domain in the Internet section, and forward 80/tcp and 443/tcp to the server's port plus the two voice ports.

Let friends connect without port forwarding (experimental)#

Server settings → Internet access → Connect without port forwarding lets friends in even when your connection is shared (CGNAT) or your router won't open ports. It works for a server hosted in the desktop app and for a standalone server (it runs the tunnel itself, see below). It's off until the owner turns it on, and marked experimental until it has been tried on more connections.

How it works. Your desktop app announces a key on HyperDHT, the public peer-to-peer network that Keet and other Pear apps use (the same idea as BitTorrent's DHT). A friend's desktop app gets the key from your invite link, looks your computer up there, and the two apps punch a path straight to each other through both routers (UDP hole punching, as game consoles and video calls do). Everything then travels inside an encrypted connection (Noise over UDX) directly between your computers: chat, files, and voice through the server's own TURN relay. Nothing of Iskra's is in between; the only fixed points are HyperDHT's three bootstrap nodes (run by Holepunch), used once to find other nodes. Iskra's own signed handshake and the invite code still decide who may join, and the server key in the link still pins your server end to end.

What to expect. From a home connection (a usual router, or a provider's shared address that follows the rules) friends can connect straight to you, including friends on mobile data. When both ends give every destination a new port (some mobile networks and strict corporate NATs), the hole punch fails and the friend can't connect yet; the switch's panel says which kind of connection you have. A relay run by a group member is planned for that case.

What it shows others. The nodes near your key on the network (anyone can run one) see your internet address and the addresses of friends who look you up, for as long as the feature is on and the key stays the same. They don't see what you host, who your members are, or anything you say. New key changes the key: old invite links then stop working this way, and members get the new one from the server by themselves. "Who Iskra talks to" in My settings lists this too.

Invite links get a fourth part, the connection key. Old three-part links keep working. Friends' apps try your address first and use the tunnel only when it can't be reached; browsers and phones can't do this yet and need a reachable address.

Under the hood. The server listens on a second port on 127.0.0.1 only (written to p2p.port in the folder), where the app's tunnel delivers friends with their real address (PROXY protocol v2), so they count as remote visitors in every way: rate limits, the security log, never the trust the server gives its own machine. Voice uses LiveKit's embedded TURN server on Voice.TurnUdpPort (default RtcUdpPort + 1) with relay ports 40000–40200, allowed to relay only to this computer; the friend's app reaches it at 127.0.0.1 through the tunnel and sends media relay-only. While your voice goes through a tunnel, the desktop app runs WebRTC with Chromium's default_public_interface_only policy (one any-address socket; with a socket per network adapter, Windows can't reach loopback) and switches back when you leave, so voice to a server on another local network (Tailscale, ZeroTier, a second router) keeps using the right adapter. The secret is in p2p.key (owner-only). Development builds and LocalOnly servers never touch the public network; tests use a private DHT on 127.0.0.1.

On a standalone server the tunnel is iskra-p2p, a second program in the server download next to iskra-server (the same tunnel code as the desktop app, packed as one Node.js single executable, about 90 MB). The server starts it while the switch is on, starts it again if it stops, and stops it with itself; there's nothing to run or install by hand. The owner turns it on in the app as above, or with "P2p": { "Enabled": true } in server.json. It joins HyperDHT on UDP port 49737 (P2p.DhtPort); no port needs to be open for it, though a firewall that lets that port in helps friends on hard NATs. If the switch's panel says iskra-p2p isn't next to the server, copy it from the download into the server's folder. iskra-p2p-licenses.txt lists what it contains. A LocalOnly server's tunnel only binds 127.0.0.1 and only joins a network named in P2p.Bootstrap (tests run a private one there).

Third-party notices (the peer-to-peer stack, bundled with the desktop app and with iskra-p2p, which also contains Node.js, MIT and the licences in its LICENSE):

Component Version License
hyperdht (Holepunch) 6.34.1 MIT
dht-rpc 6.27.0 MIT
@hyperswarm/secret-stream (Noise over UDX) 6.9.2 Apache-2.0
noise-handshake, noise-curve-ed 4.2.0, 2.1.0 Apache-2.0, ISC
udx-native (UDX streams over UDP; native addon) 1.21.3 Apache-2.0
sodium-native, sodium-universal (libsodium; native addon) 5.1.0, 5.0.1 MIT
blind-relay 1.6.1 Apache-2.0
protomux, compact-encoding, b4a, streamx and the other small Holepunch libraries they pull in as in desktop/package-lock.json MIT and Apache-2.0

Use Tailscale (free)#

Your server, your choice. Iskra charges nothing; it's just a guide.

Why you need this. Your internet provider shares one internet address between many homes (this is called CGNAT). That's normal, but it means nobody outside can reach a server on your computer, and opening ports can't fix it. Tailscale is a free app that connects your group's computers and phones as if they were on the same network, so your friends can reach your Iskra server directly.

What it costs and what it sees. Tailscale's Personal plan is free for personal, non-commercial use: up to 6 people and as many devices as you like. You share only the computer that runs your server, and each friend uses their own free Tailscale account (terms checked 2026-10-12 on tailscale.com/pricing; they can change). Tailscale sees which devices connect to which, and when, not what you say, write or share: that travels encrypted (WireGuard). It tries a direct connection first and falls back to Tailscale's relays, so it works even when everyone is behind CGNAT. Tailscale is a separate company's service: Iskra doesn't run it, isn't part of your account and never sees it, and you can remove it any time.

You (on the computer that runs the server):

  1. Install Tailscale from tailscale.com/download.
  2. Open Tailscale and sign in with Google, Microsoft, Apple or GitHub. The free Personal plan is picked for you.
  3. Share this computer with one link: on Tailscale's Machines page (login.tailscale.com), find this computer, choose Share… and copy the share link (let it be used more than once). Send it to your friends.
  4. In Iskra, open Invite friends and choose Over Tailscale (it appears once Tailscale is on), then send that invite. It points at your computer's Tailscale address, like http://100.101.102.103:47070. Server settings → Internet access shows the same address.

Each friend:

  1. Installs Tailscale from tailscale.com/download (Windows, Mac, Linux, iPhone or Android) and signs in with their own Google, Microsoft, Apple or GitHub account.
  2. Opens your share link and presses Accept. They only see your computer, nothing else.
  3. Keeps Tailscale on, opens your Iskra invite in the Iskra app and joins. Chat, voice and video work as usual.

How Iskra handles it. Iskra finds Tailscale on its own computer only from the network interfaces (an address in 100.64.0.0/10 on Tailscale's adapter: Tailscale on Windows, tailscale0 on Linux, a utun interface on macOS); it never asks Tailscale's service or app. Friends who connect over a Tailscale address (or a MagicDNS name ending in .ts.net) get voice through that same address, and voice advertises this computer's own addresses, Tailscale's included, so voice and video work over it. Friends on your home network keep using the usual invite. The link is plain HTTP, which is fine here: Tailscale encrypts the whole path, and Iskra's own end-to-end encryption for DMs and private channels works as always. Browsers need HTTPS, so friends join with the Iskra app.

If friends can't connect: check that Tailscale is on for both of you, that your share link was accepted, and that your computer is awake. Windows may ask once to allow Iskra on the network: choose Allow. You can also put the address in server.json yourself, "PublicUrl": "http://100.101.102.103:47070" (your address, or your .ts.net name): then every invite uses it, and voice still works.

Your own domain and HTTPS setup#

On a VPS, or if you'd rather set things up yourself:

  1. Ports. Open (or forward on your router) the server's port, 47070/tcp by default, and voice: 7881/tcp and 7882/udp. With HTTPS, open 80/tcp and 443/tcp instead of 47070.
  2. Address. Set PublicUrl in server.json to how friends reach you, e.g. http://203.0.113.5:47070 or https://chat.example.com. Invite links use it.
  3. HTTPS (needed for browsers). Browsers only connect to servers with HTTPS. Iskra gets a free certificate from Let's Encrypt by itself; you need a domain (or a free one from a dynamic-DNS service) pointing at your server:
JSON
"Https": { "Mode": "acme", "Domain": "chat.example.com", "Email": "you@example.com" }

Restart the server. It answers Let's Encrypt on port 80, stores the certificate in certs/, renews it automatically, and redirects plain HTTP to HTTPS. Have your own certificate? Use "Mode": "files" with CertFile and KeyFile (PEM).

Two servers on one machine (behind a proxy)#

Only one program can listen on ports 443 and 80. To run several Iskra servers on one VPS, each with its own domain, put a small reverse proxy in front: nginx reads the name the app asks for (TLS SNI) and passes the encrypted connection through untouched to that server on 127.0.0.1. Each Iskra server still gets and renews its own Let's Encrypt certificate and does TLS itself; nginx never sees inside.

So that the servers still see who's connecting (for rate limits, the security log and "is this from this machine?" checks), nginx starts each connection with a PROXY protocol header naming the client's address. With Https.ProxyProtocol on, the server's HTTPS port takes connections only from Https.ProxyTrustedFrom (default 127.0.0.1 and ::1) and only with that header (version 1 or 2); anything else is dropped. The address in the header is the client's address everywhere, and a client through the proxy never counts as this machine, even if the header says 127.0.0.1. Https.BindAddress keeps both ports on 127.0.0.1, so nobody can go around the proxy; PublicUrl stays the public address. Keep the two together: a loopback Https.BindAddress with Https.ProxyProtocol off makes every client look like this machine (one shared rate limit, no addresses in the security log), and the server warns about it at start.

Port 80 carries no server name, so it goes through nginx's http module, which picks the server by the Host header. That port only answers Let's Encrypt's check and redirects everything else to PublicUrl (webhooks sent there are refused, never redirected), so it doesn't need the client's address: leave Https.HttpProxyProtocol off for this layout. (Turn it on only if port 80 also comes through a stream proxy with proxy_protocol on, e.g. a single server behind HAProxy.)

nginx (Ubuntu: sudo apt install nginx libnginx-mod-stream, then sudo rm /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/default). Add this at the top level of /etc/nginx/nginx.conf, outside http { }:

nginx
stream {
    # Which server gets the connection: by the name in the TLS handshake (SNI).
    map $ssl_preread_server_name $iskra_upstream {
        chat.example.com       127.0.0.1:9443;
        community.example.com  127.0.0.1:8443;
        default                127.0.0.1:9443;
    }
    server {
        listen 443;
        listen [::]:443;
        ssl_preread on;          # read the name, don't decrypt
        proxy_pass $iskra_upstream;
        proxy_protocol on;       # tell the server who the client is (PROXY protocol v1)
        proxy_timeout 10m;       # idle limit; Iskra pings every 20 seconds
    }
}

and /etc/nginx/sites-available/iskra (link it into sites-enabled/):

nginx
server {
    listen 80;
    listen [::]:80;
    server_name chat.example.com;
    location / { proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:9080; proxy_set_header Host $host; }
}
server {
    listen 80;
    listen [::]:80;
    server_name community.example.com;
    location / { proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8080; proxy_set_header Host $host; }
}

The first server's server.json:

JSON
{
  "Name": "Chat",
  "Port": 47070,                       // internal, localhost only: each server needs its own
  "PublicUrl": "https://chat.example.com",
  "Https": {
    "Mode": "acme", "Domain": "chat.example.com", "Email": "you@example.com",
    "Port": 9443, "HttpPort": 9080,
    "BindAddress": "127.0.0.1",
    "ProxyProtocol": true
  },
  "Voice": { "Port": 7880, "RtcTcpPort": 7881, "RtcUdpPort": 7882 }
}

The second one's:

JSON
{
  "Name": "Community",
  "Port": 47071,
  "PublicUrl": "https://community.example.com",
  "Https": {
    "Mode": "acme", "Domain": "community.example.com", "Email": "you@example.com",
    "Port": 8443, "HttpPort": 8080,
    "BindAddress": "127.0.0.1",
    "ProxyProtocol": true
  },
  "Voice": { "Port": 7890, "RtcTcpPort": 7891, "RtcUdpPort": 7892 }
}

Each server needs its own folder, its own Port, HTTPS ports and voice ports (Voice.Port is LiveKit's local API). Voice media doesn't go through nginx: open each server's RtcTcpPort/tcp and RtcUdpPort/udp in the firewall (here 7881, 7882, 7891, 7892) along with 80/tcp and 443/tcp. Both domains must point straight at the machine (DNS only: a CDN proxy in front would end the TLS passthrough). Set PublicUrl to the public address without the internal port, or invites and redirects would name :9443. Start the servers, then sudo nginx -t && sudo systemctl reload nginx; each server gets its certificate through nginx on port 80 within a minute and renews it the same way. If the proxy is set up wrongly (no proxy_protocol on, or it connects from an address not in ProxyTrustedFrom), the server drops those connections and says so in its log, at most once a minute.

Ports at a glance#

Port What When
47070/tcp (Port) The server: app, invites, uploads, voice signaling, webhooks. Speaks HTTP and HTTPS on the same port. Always
80/tcp → server port Let's Encrypt's check, and redirects to HTTPS Let friends anywhere join, or Https on
443/tcp → server port HTTPS for friends Let friends anywhere join, or Https on
7881/tcp, 7882/udp Voice and video media (RtcTcpPort, RtcUdpPort) Always, for voice from outside your network
7880 LiveKit's local API Never exposed

Push notifications#

Nothing to set up. On first start the server makes its push key (vapid.json) and sends notifications for mentions, replies, DMs, group chats, calls and event reminders through the browsers' own push services (an outgoing HTTPS connection). Members turn them on per device in My settings → Notifications; on phones that needs the web app over HTTPS, and on iPhone and iPad the app added to the Home Screen. The phone apps show notifications while they're open.

Voice, stages and watch parties#

Voice channels, stages, DM and group calls and watch parties all use the same voice service (LiveKit), which the server starts and stops by itself: nothing extra to run or open beyond the voice ports above. Stages are voice channels where the server tells LiveKit who may speak. A watch party only shares a clock through the server; everyone's app plays the video from its source (YouTube, a link, or a file uploaded to your server, which then serves it to everyone watching). A party can queue what plays next (up to 100 items; uploads in the queue count as in use) and run audio-only as a jukebox.

Join-to-create rooms: tick Join to create a room in a voice channel's settings to make it a lobby. Nobody stays in a lobby: whoever joins gets a voice room of their own right under it ("alice's-room"), with the lobby's permissions and user limit. The host can rename it, set a limit and lock it (then only people they invite, or a moderator moves in, can join); the room is removed about 30 seconds after the last person leaves. Only the lobby setting itself is in the audit log.

GIFs#

The GIF picker uses KLIPY (Google closed Tenor's API in June 2026). It's off until an admin adds a key:

  1. Sign up at the KLIPY Partner Panel and create an API key for your server. Leave ads off.
  2. In Iskra: Server settings → GIFs, paste the key and click Turn on.

There are two modes:

  • Through this server (the default): your server searches KLIPY and passes the GIFs along, so members' devices never contact KLIPY: it only sees your server, and the key never leaves it. It uses your server's bandwidth for every GIF shown. KLIPY's standard terms describe apps calling KLIPY directly; if you want their written OK for proxying, ask developers@klipy.com.
  • Straight from KLIPY (only if you pick it): members' apps search KLIPY and load GIFs from KLIPY themselves, so KLIPY sees their IP addresses and searches. The key is shared with your members' apps, which is fine for a key made just for your server. GIFs in messages load when clicked, unless someone turned on auto-load for their device (My settings → Appearance).

Everything else Iskra and your server talk to is listed in Who Iskra talks to.

To turn GIFs off, click Turn off there.

Live captions#

Members can turn on live captions in calls. The speech recognition runs on their own devices, but the speech model (Whisper base, about 78 MB) comes from your server: the first time someone turns captions on, your server downloads it once from Hugging Face (at a pinned version, every byte checked against pinned SHA-256 hashes) into the models/ folder, and serves it to members' apps from then on. So their devices only talk to your server, and Hugging Face only sees your server, once. Only members get it: their app asks your server for a short-lived link first, so nobody else can download it from your server or make it fetch the model. It takes about 78 MB of disk space (plan for 100 MB). The security log notes the download. To not offer captions at all, set "Captions": { "ModelDownload": false } in server.json and restart; the apps then say this server doesn't offer captions. Deleting models/ is safe: it's fetched again the next time someone needs it.

The link is valid for an hour and only for that member; the app asks for a new one whenever it needs it. Apps from before 2.0.0-alpha.13 download the model without a link, so an updated server refuses them: members who want captions need an up-to-date app. How the link works: PROTOCOL.md; what runs on members' devices: Voice processing.

Bots and webhooks#

Everything here is in Server settings → Bots & webhooks, for admins. Nothing runs or connects until an admin turns it on. The details, and how to write your own bot: Bots and webhooks.

  • Built-in bots (the Bots tab): Dice (/roll 2d6+3), Polls (/poll Question | Answer | Answer) and Reminders (/remind me in 10m …) run inside your server, so there's nothing to install or keep running. Turn one on and it joins as a bot member; change its role or the channel's overrides to choose where it answers. They read only their own commands and don't answer in encrypted channels.
  • Your own bots (the Bots tab): make a single-use bot invite and start the bot with it. Leave Can read all messages off unless the bot needs to read along: then it gets only its commands, button clicks and forms, and messages that mention it or reply to it. You can change this later. Bots that joined before this choice existed keep reading everything until you turn it off.
  • Webhooks (incoming): a secret URL that posts into one channel, for anything that can post to Discord, and GitHub.
  • Outgoing webhooks (the Outgoing tab): your server sends chosen events (new messages or reactions in the channels you pick, people joining or leaving, events starting) as signed JSON to an https:// address you choose, such as a Minecraft bridge or Home Assistant. Each one has its own signing secret (shown once; New secret makes another), a log of the last 50 deliveries and Send a test. Your server makes these requests, so the address sees your server's IP address and what the event contains (message text and names); nothing from encrypted channels, DMs or group chats is ever sent. Addresses on your own network (http:// allowed there) are refused unless the owner ticks Allow addresses on my own network for that webhook. A webhook that keeps failing is turned off, and admins who are online are told. At most 10 per server. Every member sees where their server sends things under My settings → Privacy & data → Who Iskra talks to. The secrets are stored in the server's database, so they're in its backups too: keep backups private, and make a new secret if one leaks.

Backups, moving and importing#

Backups#

Download one: as the owner, open Server settings → Backup & move, choose a passphrase and click Make backup. You get one file (<name>-<date>.iskrabackup) with everything: messages, channels, members, roles, files, settings and the server's key. It's made while the server keeps running.

Because the file holds the server's key, it's always encrypted with your passphrase (Argon2id and XChaCha20-Poly1305 from libsodium). Keep the file and the passphrase in different places: without the passphrase nobody can open it, and nobody can recover it for you either.

Daily backups: every day the server also keeps a copy of the database, settings and keys in its own backups/ folder (the last 7), so a bad disk write or a mistake can be undone. These aren't encrypted, since they sit next to the keys anyway (owner-only file permissions on Linux and macOS). Uploaded files stay in uploads/; turn on Include uploaded files if you want them copied too. Change this in Server settings → Backup & move or in server.json → Backups. A daily backup only helps while that disk is fine, so download one now and then as well, or copy them to another disk:

Copy daily backups to another disk, encrypted: in Server settings → Backup & move → Also copy them to (or server.json → Backups → CopyTo and CopyPassphrase), give a folder on the server's computer that lives on another disk: a USB stick mounted at /mnt/usb/iskra, a second drive, or a network share (an SMB/NFS mount on Linux, a share like \\nas\iskra or a mapped drive on Windows), and a passphrase (at least 8 characters). After each daily backup the server encrypts it with that passphrase, in the same format as a downloaded backup, and writes it there as auto-YYYY-MM-DD.iskrabackup (to a temporary name first, then renamed, so a half-written copy never looks finished), keeping the same number of days there; it only ever deletes files named auto-YYYY-MM-DD.iskrabackup, so use a folder of its own for each server. Copies are never written unencrypted: without a passphrase the setting is refused. The passphrase is kept in server.json (whoever can read the server's disk has its key anyway; the passphrase protects the stick or share) and is never shown, logged or sent back to the app. Keep it somewhere safe too, like a password manager: restoring a copy asks for it (Restoring). The path must be absolute and outside the server's folder, and the folder must already exist and be writable by the server's user (on Linux: sudo mkdir -p /mnt/usb/iskra && sudo chown iskra:iskra /mnt/usb/iskra). The server never creates it, so a stick that isn't mounted doesn't quietly fill the main disk: the copy fails, Server settings → Backup & move shows why, and it tries again within the hour. A failed copy never stops the server or the daily backup. Mount a stick that's always plugged in by UUID with nofail in /etc/fstab, so the computer still starts without it.

From the command line (this works while the server runs, too):

shell
iskra-server backup my-server my-server.iskrabackup      # asks for a passphrase

Backup buddies (a friend's server)#

A daily backup on the same computer doesn't help if that computer is lost. Backup buddies send each daily backup to a friend's Iskra server instead, and you can do the same for them. Nothing goes through Iskra or anyone else: your server talks to your friend's directly.

  1. Your friend opens Server settings → Backup & move → Keep backups for a friend, names the spot, picks how much space it gets (2 GB by default), how many copies to keep (3, at least 3) and how long to keep them after either of you stops (7 days), and clicks Make a spot. They send you the pairing code it shows (iskra-buddy:…, single use, 24 hours).
  2. You paste it in Server settings → Backup & move → Backup buddies and click Add backup buddy. The first time, your server makes a recovery code (XXXXX-XXXXX-XXXXX-XXXXX-XXXXX) and shows it: save it in a password manager or on paper, away from this computer. It's the only key to the copies (Show recovery code shows it again while the server runs).
  3. After each daily backup (or Back up now) your server encrypts the backup with the recovery code (the same format as a downloaded backup) and sends it in 4 MB parts that resume after a cut, at most 1 MB/s by default (server.json → BuddyBackups → UploadKbPerSecond, 0 = no limit). A failed copy is tried again after 1, 5, 15, 60 and 180 minutes, then every 6 hours; Backup buddies shows the last copy, its size and any problem.

Your friend's server only ever holds encrypted blobs in buddy-held/ in its folder (never in its own backups), with their size and time: it can't read them, and never opens or runs them. It keeps the newest copies within the space it gave you, takes at most 3 copies a day from you, and only from your server (every request is signed with your server's key). It always keeps one older copy besides the newest (the newest one that's at least 2 days old, or else the oldest), whatever else arrives, so a server someone took over can't push out every good copy. Either of you can stop at any time: the copies stay for the grace period (at least a day when you stop, so a server someone took over can't wipe its own backups; your friend can delete at once), then they're deleted.

What it needs: your server must be able to reach your friend's at its address (just the server, like https://friend.example.com, no path). That's your friend's internet address if they Let friends anywhere join, or a local or Tailscale address (plain http:// only works on local networks; https:// everywhere else). A server that's only reachable through Connect without port forwarding can't hold backups for others.

What it protects against: a lost or broken computer, a dead disk, a fire. What it doesn't: someone who takes over your server can read your messages anyway, and also has the recovery code (your server keeps it to encrypt every day), so they could read the copies at your friend's too, or send junk that pushes out the newer good copies (at most 3 a day). That older protected copy stays, and they can't make your friend delete anything early.

Restoring#

  • Desktop app: Create a server → Restore from a backup, pick the file and enter the passphrase. The server starts on this computer with everything it had, on free ports and this network's address. To get it back from a backup buddy, choose From a buddy's server and give your friend's server address and your recovery code: the newest copy is downloaded, checked and restored. The restored server keeps its buddies and carries on sending them backups.

  • Standalone server:

    shell
    iskra-server restore my-server.iskrabackup my-server    # asks for the passphrase
iskra-server my-server

    The folder must be new or empty: a restore never overwrites a server. Daily backups (backups/auto-*.zip) restore the same way, without a passphrase. Check Port and PublicUrl in server.json if the new machine's address is different. HTTPS certificates aren't in backups; the new machine gets its own.

For scripts, --passphrase-stdin reads the passphrase from standard input (or set ISKRA_BACKUP_PASSPHRASE).

From a backup buddy, on the command line:

shell
iskra-server restore-buddy https://friend.example.com --list          # the copies there (asks for the recovery code)
iskra-server restore-buddy https://friend.example.com my-server       # restores the newest one (--version <id> for another)

--code-stdin reads the recovery code from standard input (or set ISKRA_BUDDY_RECOVERY_CODE). A copy downloaded any other way restores with iskra-server restore, with the recovery code as the passphrase.

Moving a server to another computer#

Use Server settings → Backup & move → Move this server. It walks you through it:

  1. Back up this server.
  2. Restore the backup on the new computer (as above) and start it there. If friends join from outside your home, turn on Let friends anywhere join there, or set up HTTPS.
  3. Enter the new address. Iskra connects to it and checks that it really is this server (it has the same key).
  4. Move everyone. The old copy publishes a notice, "this server moved to <new address>", signed with the server's key. Everyone's app checks the signature against the key it already trusts and switches to the new address by itself; people who are offline get it the next time they connect. From then on the old copy refuses new messages, so nothing gets lost in it.

Keep the old copy running for a few days so everyone gets the notice, then stop it, and share new invite links from the new address. Changed your mind? iskra-server move <old-folder> --cancel takes the notice down. With the old server stopped, iskra-server move <old-folder> <new-address> publishes one.

Members and their roles, channels and history all come along, because the server's identity travels with it. Direct messages are end-to-end encrypted: their envelopes come along too, and everyone's app keeps its own history.

Importing from Discord#

Bring your Discord server's history along with DiscordChatExporter:

  1. Export the channels you want in the JSON format. Turn on Download assets (--media on the command line) to include files and profile pictures.
  2. Zip the folder it made, or use a single .json file.
  3. As the owner, open Server settings → Import from Discord and upload it. A progress bar shows how it's going, and you can keep chatting meanwhile.

Each Discord channel becomes a channel here (threads become threads), with its messages in order, their dates, replies, pins, files and reaction counts. Messages show their authors' Discord names and pictures with an Imported from Discord label: those people aren't accounts here, and nobody can edit those messages. Tick read-only archive to keep the imported channels for reading only. Each channel's Discord category is kept with it.

What doesn't come along: roles and permissions (DiscordChatExporter can't export them, so set up roles here and invite your friends), direct messages, and files that weren't downloaded with the export (their names are shown instead; Iskra never fetches anything from Discord). The upload is checked like any other: zip entries can't point outside the export, every file is typed by its content, and there are size limits (Import.MaxMb, 4 GB by default).

From the command line, best with the server stopped:

shell
iskra-server import-discord my-server export.zip              # add --read-only for an archive

Exporting channels#

Admins (and anyone whose role has Export channels) can download channels to keep or share outside Iskra, like DiscordChatExporter does for Discord. Open Server settings → Export channels, tick the channels, optionally pick a date range, and choose whether to include files and images and threads. The server builds a zip in the background (you'll see its progress, and you can keep chatting); then Download it. The link works for an hour, then the file is deleted from the server.

In the zip, each channel has its own folder with:

  • channel.html: open it in any browser to read the channel as it looked: names, times, replies, reactions, pins, polls, threads, forum posts and docs pages, with images shown inline. It works offline and loads nothing from the internet (it has no scripts at all, and a strict content security policy).
  • channel.json: the same content for programs, in a documented, versioned format (see "Channel export" in the protocol reference).
  • attachments/: the files and images posted there (if you included them).

What's never exported: end-to-end encrypted channels (the server can't read them; they can only be exported from a member's device), direct messages and group chats, deleted messages and disappearing messages. People appear under their display name at export time; account keys aren't included. Each export is noted in the activity log and the security log (which channels and dates, never what was in them). A zip can be at most 1 GB: leave out files or pick a shorter range for bigger channels. One export runs at a time per server.

server.json reference#

JSON
{
  "Name": "Game Night",
  "Port": 47070,                       // the server's port: HTTP, plus HTTPS when open to the internet (localhost-only with Https on)
  "PublicUrl": null,                   // how friends reach the server; default http://localhost:<Port>, or https://<Domain>
  "AppUrl": "https://app.iskra.foo",   // the web app invite links open
  "Template": null,                    // starter template applied once to a new server: "gaming", "friends", "tabletop", "empty" or a .json path
  "OwnerClaim": null,                  // one-time owner key from "Rent a small server" (moved out of this file on first start), or "generate" for a claim code (DigitalOcean Marketplace)
  "MaxUploadMb": 512,                  // largest file a member may upload (also in the app: Server settings → Limits)
  "UploadQuota": {                     // per account, over any 24 hours; 0 = no limit (admins and the owner have none)
    "MemberMbPerDay": 10240,           // members and trusted
    "GuestMbPerDay": 1024
  },
  "Limits": {                          // 0 = no limit (uploads still can't exceed MaxUploadMb)
    "SoundMaxSeconds": 0,              // soundboard sound length
    "SoundMaxMb": 0,
    "EmojiMaxKb": 1024,
    "StickerMaxKb": 4096
  },
  "LocalOnly": false,                  // true: listen on localhost only (testing; nobody else can connect)
  "Voice": {
    "Enabled": true,
    "LiveKitPath": null,               // default: next to iskra-server, then $ISKRA_LIVEKIT, then PATH
    "Port": 7880,                      // LiveKit's local API (not exposed; voice signaling goes through the server port)
    "RtcTcpPort": 7881,
    "RtcUdpPort": 7882,
    "ClientUrl": null,                 // override the voice URL clients use (default <PublicUrl>/livekit)
    "TurnUdpPort": 0,                  // LiveKit's TURN for friends through the p2p tunnel; 0 = RtcUdpPort + 1
    "TurnRelayStart": 40000, "TurnRelayEnd": 40200
  },
  "P2p": {                             // "Connect without port forwarding" (Server settings → Internet access)
    "Enabled": false,
    "TunnelPort": 0,                   // the tunnel's listener on 127.0.0.1; 0 = any free port, written to p2p.port
    "SidecarPath": null,               // standalone server: iskra-p2p (null = next to iskra-server, or ISKRA_P2P_SIDECAR)
    "Bootstrap": null,                 // DHT bootstrap nodes "host:port,..." (null = HyperDHT's public ones)
    "DhtPort": 0                       // the tunnel's UDP port on the DHT; 0 = 49737
  },
  "Https": {
    "Mode": "off",                     // "off" | "acme" (Let's Encrypt) | "files"
    "Domain": null,
    "Email": null,
    "CertFile": null, "KeyFile": null, // PEM, for "files"
    "Port": 443,
    "HttpPort": 80,                    // Let's Encrypt's check; everything else redirects to PublicUrl
    "BindAddress": null,               // listen on this address only, e.g. "127.0.0.1" behind a proxy; null = every interface
    "ProxyProtocol": false,            // Port takes only connections from ProxyTrustedFrom that start with a PROXY protocol header (v1 or v2)
    "HttpProxyProtocol": false,        // the same for HttpPort (only behind a stream proxy on port 80)
    "ProxyTrustedFrom": ["127.0.0.1", "::1"] // the proxy's addresses (see Two servers on one machine)
  },
  "Internet": {                        // "Let friends anywhere join" (Server settings → Internet access)
    "Enabled": false,
    "Domain": null,                    // your own domain pointing at your network; default <ip>.sslip.io
    "DnsSuffix": "sslip.io",
    "PortMapping": true                // ask the router to open ports (UPnP / NAT-PMP); false to forward them yourself
  },
  "Backups": {                         // daily backups in backups/ (Server settings → Backup & move)
    "Enabled": true,
    "Keep": 7,                         // how many days to keep (1–30)
    "IncludeUploads": false,           // also copy uploads/ into each one
    "CopyTo": null,                    // also copy each one, encrypted, into this folder on another disk, e.g. "/mnt/usb/iskra"
    "CopyPassphrase": null             // the copies' passphrase (set it in the app; never shown again)
  },
  "BuddyBackups": {                    // backup buddies (set them up in the app)
    "UploadKbPerSecond": 1024          // how fast copies go to friends' servers; 0 = no limit
  },
  "Import": {
    "MaxMb": 4096                      // largest Discord export the owner may upload
  },
  "Updates": {                         // Server settings → Server updates (see Updating)
    "Mode": "notify",                  // "off" | "notify" (tell the owner) | "auto" (also install; Linux with systemd)
    "Channel": "stable",               // "stable" | "prerelease" (also test versions)
    "Window": "04:00",                 // automatic installs start within the hour after this (server time)
    "VerifyAttestation": true          // only install releases whose build attestation verifies (older "RequireAttestation" is ignored)
  },
  "Retention": {                       // how long data is kept, in days; 0 = forever (Server settings → Sign-ins & security)
    "MessagesDays": 0,                 // channel messages, and encrypted DM and group envelopes
    "UploadsDays": 0,                  // files in messages and DMs (avatars, emoji, stickers, sounds and event covers stay)
    "AuditDays": 90,                   // the audit log
    "SecurityLogDays": 365,            // the security log
    "SecurityLogIps": false            // also record IP addresses in the security log
  },
  "Captions": {                        // live captions (see Live captions)
    "ModelDownload": true              // offer the speech model (~78 MB, fetched once from Hugging Face into models/)
  },
  "BugInbox": {
    "Accept": false                    // only for the server that receives Iskra's bug reports; leave it off
  },
  "Logs": {                            // the server's own log files in logs/ (see Logs)
    "PlainDays": 60,                   // days a file stays plain text (1–365)
    "KeepDays": 180,                   // days a file is kept at all, gzipped after PlainDays (1–365)
    "MaxMb": 200,                      // all log files together (10–2000); over it, the oldest go first
    "Debug": false                     // also write debug lines (for developers)
  }
}

What's in the folder#

File What it is
server.json Settings (above)
server.key The server's identity. Invite links pin it, so clients know they reach the real server. Keep it secret, keep it with the folder.
iskra.db Members, channels, messages, roles, invites, direct-message envelopes (encrypted end to end)
uploads/ Uploaded files (including avatars, custom emoji and soundboard sounds), stored once per unique content
livekit.key Keys between the server and its voice service (handed to LiveKit in its environment, never on the command line)
vapid.json The server's push-notification key. Keep it with the folder: if it's lost, a new one is made and members turn notifications on again.
certs/ HTTPS certificates and the Let's Encrypt account (when HTTPS is on, or open to the internet)
owner-invite.txt The one-time owner link, until the owner has joined
owner-claim The one-time owner key from "Rent a small server" or a claim code, until the owner has joined
owner-claim-code.txt The claim code and when it expires (DigitalOcean Marketplace), until the owner has joined
p2p.key, p2p.port The key friends' invites carry for "Connect without port forwarding" (owner-only), and the port of the tunnel's listener on 127.0.0.1 (written at each start)
backups/ Daily backups (auto-YYYY-MM-DD.zip, not encrypted), briefly a backup being downloaded, and the encrypted copy for backup buddies (buddy-*.iskrabackup)
buddy-held/ Encrypted backups this server keeps for friends' servers (backup buddies); never in this server's own backups
moved.json The signed "this server moved" notice, after Move this server
logs/ The server's log: one file per day (YYYY-MM-DD.log, UTC), gzipped after 60 days, deleted after 180 (see Logs)
server.log Only error output (why it couldn't start, a crash), when the desktop app or autostart runs the server; emptied at start once it's over 5 MB
exports/ "Download my data" files while their 10-minute link lasts (never in backups)
models/ The live-captions speech model, once someone has used captions (about 78 MB; never in backups, fetched again when needed)

Profile pages, polls, threads, pins, forums, events, roles, groups (their encrypted messages), webhooks (only a hash of each secret), outgoing webhooks (with their signing secrets), built-in bots and push subscriptions are all in iskra.db too, so copying the folder takes everything along.

On Linux and macOS the server creates the folder (and certs/) readable by its own user only, writes secrets as 0600, and tightens older secret files to 0600 when it starts.

Uploads that nothing uses (no message, DM, avatar, emoji, sticker, sound, webhook, event cover, profile page or running watch party) are deleted after a day.

Security log and retention: the owner reads the server's security log in Server settings → Sign-ins & security (failed sign-ins, new members and devices, key changes, account deletions, backups, moves, data downloads; IP addresses only if you turn that on) and sets how long messages, files, the audit log and the security log are kept. Deleting happens every hour and can't be undone. Members download what the server keeps about them in Settings → Privacy & data; if someone asks you instead, use Someone's data in Server settings → Sign-ins & security.

Backups and moving: see Backups, moving and importing. Copying the stopped server's folder works too; it holds secrets (server.key, vapid.json, livekit.key, certs/, backups/), so keep copies private. Updating: see Updating. Automatic updates keep their state in .update/ next to iskra-server, not in the world folder.

Logs#

The server writes its log itself, into logs/ in its folder: one file per day (2026-10-17.log, UTC days), the same lines it prints on its console (or to journalctl under systemd). Each line is one event:

2026-10-17T13:41:30.112Z INFO  srv   sess   closed      SES-120 conn=k3f acct=4be1d9 close=1000 why=kicked dur=6.9s

time (UTC), level, who wrote it (srv the server, lk voice, p2p the tunnel, hook webhooks), area, event, a code for problems, then details. Codes and what to do about each: log-codes.md. The line format in full: development.md, Logs.

What's never in it: names (people's, channels', webhooks', files'), message text, keys, tokens, invite or p2p secrets, claim codes, IP addresses and file paths. People appear as acct= (a short code that only matches up inside this server's log) and each connection as conn=, an id the member's app is told too. So you can share a log with someone helping you.

How long it's kept: files stay plain for 60 days, are gzipped (.log.gz) until 180 days, then deleted; and all of logs/ together stays under 200 MB, the oldest files going first. Set Logs in server.json to change that. Trimming runs at start and once a day. The startup lines list the version, ports, voice, p2p and these settings.

The desktop app's own log. The desktop app keeps a log of its own in the same format, in its data folder: %APPDATA%\iskra-desktop\logs on Windows, ~/Library/Application Support/iskra-desktop/logs on macOS and ~/.config/iskra-desktop/logs on Linux (one YYYY-MM-DD.log per UTC day). It has the app's start and stop, its windows and tray, sleep and wake, a page or helper process that stopped (DSK-110), the servers it hosts starting and stopping (by port, with their exit code: DSK-120), update checks (upd), and the app page's own lines (app: connections to each server with its srv= and conn= ids, voice joins and why they ended, errors). Same rules: no names, message text, keys, tokens, addresses or paths. It's kept like the server's (plain 60 days, gzipped until 180, then deleted) and under 50 MB in all. A server hosted in the app writes its own log in logs/ in its server folder. Report a bug in the desktop app adds the last 30 minutes of this log to the report, so a host can match a member's report with the server's log by srv= and conn=.

Public page#

Opening the server's address in a browser shows its public page (Server settings → Overview → Public page). Off by default it shows nothing about your server, only that it's an Iskra server and where to get the app; turned on, you pick what it shows: name, picture, banner, a short description, the start of the rules, a rounded member count and a Join button for an invite you choose. The apps still read the same JSON at /, which includes the server's name and icon for invite previews.

Server icon and banner#

Server settings → Overview → Icon and banner (the owner and admins; a server can give or take that power per built-in role under Roles). The icon is square (at least 128×128 pixels, up to 1 MB) and shows in everyone's server list, the server's header and menu, and on invite links before people join. The banner is wide (2.5 to 4 times as wide as it is high, for example 960×360, up to 3 MB) and shows above the channel list. PNG, JPEG or WebP, still pictures only. The app lets you crop either before it uploads; everyone sees the change at once.

The server checks every picture itself and takes out its metadata (EXIF with GPS positions, text, comments, thumbnails) before anyone sees it. Invite pages only ever get the icon, from /icon on your server: no banner, no names, no channels. Both are in your backups with the other uploads. The server's name still comes from Name in server.json.

Roles and moderation#

Everyone has a base role: Guest < Member < Trusted < Admin < Owner. Each channel has a base role needed to see it and one needed to post (or speak, in voice). Admins can kick and ban people ranked below them and hand out base roles below their own; the owner can do everything. Invite links can carry a base role and expire after 1 hour to 30 days, optionally single use. What each base role may do is adjustable under Server settings → Roles (for example, members may by default use emoji and stickers from their other servers here: their app copies the picture into your server, which keeps up to 300 such emoji and 100 stickers, the same picture once; turn that off per role if you don't want it).

On top of the base roles, admins can make custom roles (Server settings → Roles) with a name, colour and icon, and give them permissions such as managing messages, timing people out, kicking, banning, managing channels or roles, muting and moving people in voice, or mentioning everyone. Roles can also change what a channel allows (per-channel overrides), and roles can be made mentionable. Moderators have timeouts, slowmode per channel, server mute and move in voice, and an audit log of moderation actions (kept 90 days).

Letting people in: an invite can be made with Approve each person who joins: whoever opens it waits outside (they see only the server's name and icon) until a moderator lets them in or turns them away under Server settings → Reports; moderators see the name, which invite and since when, never an address. Admins can pause invites (Server settings → AutoMod → Joining, or the banner in the invite dialog) so every link stops letting people in until resumed, and set a newcomer slowmode: members younger than N hours wait at least X seconds between messages in every channel. AutoMod's Join flood rule pauses invites by itself when more than N people join within M minutes and posts an alert; resuming is always by hand. All of it lands in the activity log.

A picture per server: next to the server nickname (server menu → Server nickname…, or a member's sheet), anyone can set a picture shown instead of their profile picture on that server only, with the same crop and limits as the profile picture (1 MB; the server stores a copy without metadata). Admins can change it for members below them. It goes when the member leaves.

Moderators' tools: Select messages… in a message's menu ticks up to 100 messages in a channel and deletes them in one go (one activity-log entry); in an encrypted channel only the stored copies go. Banning offers Also delete their messages from the last 24 hours / 7 days. A member's sheet has a Warning (the person sees it at once), private Moderator notes and their Moderation history; People who left at the bottom of Server settings → Members lists recent leaves, kicks and bans so a report about someone who's gone can still end in a ban, and keeps their notes and history; entries are kept 90 days (the activity log's horizon), the name removed earlier if the account is deleted.

Roles members pick themselves: tick Members can pick this role themselves on a role (for platforms, interests, ping lists; such a role can never carry permissions or count as rank), then write the questions under Server settings → Onboarding: a title, an optional question, one or several answers, and the roles to pick from. New members answer right after agreeing to the rules; everyone can change their picks later from Pick your roles in the server menu or with /roles. Give one of these roles view on a channel to make an opt-in channel. Templates carry them as selfAssign and roleGroups (templates).
